description_en: Marcus Licinius Crassus was born into a wealthy senatorial family in Rome around 115 BCE.
Crassus' father and brother were killed during the Marian-Cinnan proscriptions, and Crassus fled to Hispania.
Crassus amassed his fortune through proscription purchases, real estate speculation, a fire brigade that extorted property owners, silver mines, and slave trading.
Crassus was appointed commander against Spartacus in 72 BCE after several Roman armies had been defeated.
Crassus defeated Spartacus in 71 BCE and crucified approximately 6,000 survivors along the Appian Way.
Crassus served as consul in 70 BCE alongside Pompey.
Crassus formed the informal political alliance known as the First Triumvirate with Caesar and Pompey in 60 BCE.
Crassus served as consul for the second time in 55 BCE, with Pompey as his colleague.
Crassus was appointed governor of Syria in 54 BCE and used the position to launch an invasion of Parthia.
Crassus was defeated and killed at the Battle of Carrhae in 53 BCE by the Parthian general Surena.
Crassus' death at Carrhae destabilized the First Triumvirate, contributing to the eventual civil war between Caesar and Pompey.
Crassus was known for his extraordinary wealth, with Plutarch estimating his net worth at approximately 7,100 talents.
Crassus supported Julius Caesar financially, including paying off Caesar's substantial debts.
Crassus had two sons: Marcus, who served under Caesar in Gaul, and Publius, who died at Carrhae.
Crassus was married to Tertulla, about whom little is known in the historical record.
Plutarch reports that the Parthians poured molten gold down Crassus' throat after his death as a symbol of his greed.
